mcqs.question: What's the core design decision behind a good on-call and paging design?
options: Page every team in the organization for every alert to ensure nothing is missed
Rely on whoever happens to be available at the moment an alert fires, regardless of ownership
Route alerts randomly across the on-call roster to balance load evenly
Route alerts to the team that owns the failing component, with a clear, time-boxed escalation path if unacknowledged
mcqs.explanation: Ownership-based routing is the foundation everything else builds on — rotation size and escalation timers only matter once the right team is being paged in the first place. Paging everyone, whoever's available, or a random roster all skip the actual design decision.

mcqs.question: Why did routing checkout alerts directly to the checkout team cut response time from 12 minutes to under 2?
options: The checkout team was simply faster at fixing bugs than other teams
Direct, ownership-based routing eliminated the time a generic on-call engineer previously spent figuring out who actually owned the failing component
The alert threshold itself was lowered to trigger earlier
The checkout service became more reliable overall as a result
mcqs.explanation: The scenario attributes the entire 10-minute gap to routing, not to responders being inherently faster once paged. It wasn't a threshold change or a reliability improvement — it was eliminating the time spent identifying the right owner.

mcqs.question: An alert fires for a shared dependency that three teams depend on — who should be paged?
options: Page the team that owns the shared dependency, and notify (not page) the affected teams so they have visibility without diluting responsibility
Page all three dependent teams simultaneously so each can attempt its own fix
Page only the most senior engineer available across all three teams
Suppress the alert entirely since ownership across three teams is ambiguous
mcqs.explanation: Only the owning team can actually fix the dependency — paging the three consumers creates uncoordinated, duplicated response without adding fixing power. Notifying them keeps visibility without diluting who's responsible for the fix.

mcqs.question: Why does a single catch-all on-call rotation guarantee slower incident response than ownership-based routing?
options: A single catch-all rotation is always faster to respond than per-team routing
Ownership-based routing is only useful for organizations with more than 20 engineers
Whoever's paged in a catch-all setup must first identify which component failed and who actually owns it before they can start fixing anything
Catch-all rotations eliminate the need for any escalation policy at all
mcqs.explanation: The delay in a catch-all setup comes from the extra step of figuring out ownership before work can even start — exactly the 12-minute gap seen in the checkout scenario. It isn't inherently faster, isn't limited to large orgs, and still needs an escalation policy.
